artiest/emmanuel-pahud.text:
Emmanuel Pahud is a Swiss flautist, born in Geneva in 1970. His father is of French-Swiss descent and his mother is French. He grew up in a family without musicians, and because his father worked for an American company, the family moved often. As a boy in Italy he became fascinated by the flute. He received his first flute for Christmas and took lessons with Philippe Binet and then with Philippe's father, François. In 1978 the family moved to Brussels, where he studied at the music academy in Uccle. From the age of four until he was twenty-two, his teachers included François Binet, Carlos Bruneel and Aurèle Nicolet.

He trained at the Conservatoire de Paris and broke through internationally when he joined the Berliner Philharmoniker in 1992. He is also a soloist, and has made recordings of Mozart's flute concertos and the Concerto for Flute and Harp, of Debussy, Ravel and Prokofiev, and of Brazilian melodies on Tico-Tico (2000). His other albums include Cantos y danzas (1998), Paris (1998) and Quatuors avec flûte (1999). The Guardian wrote that he heralded the arrival of a new master of the flute.

Pahud plays Baroque, classical, jazz and contemporary music, and is known for his versatility and his clear, agile tone. He shows that the flute is not only an orchestral instrument but also a solo voice that can move between genres.
artiest/emmanuel-pahud.listen: Listen to Debussy's Syrinx in a recording by Emmanuel Pahud and notice the long, calm lines and the silence between the phrases. Can you hear how the tone of the flute sounds almost like a soft breath?

artiest/emmanuelle-haim.text:
Emmanuelle Haïm is a French harpsichordist and conductor with a special interest in early music and the Baroque. She was born in Paris in 1962 and had her first musical experience when her father bought a grand piano. For thirteen years she studied at the Conservatoire in Paris, where she learned the organ with André Isoir and the harpsichord with Kenneth Gilbert and Christophe Rousset. She won five first prizes. William Christie then invited her to work with Les Arts Florissants.

After a few years she left Les Arts Florissants to become a conductor. In 2000 she founded her own Baroque ensemble, Le Concert d'Astrée, with which she performs regularly. In 2001 she made her debut as a conductor with Glyndebourne Touring Opera in Handel's Rodelinda, which made her name. In 2006 she returned to Glyndebourne for Giulio Cesare, and in 2008 she conducted at the Proms for the first time. Her recordings include Dido and Aeneas (2003), L'Orfeo (2004), Delirio (2005), Il trionfo del Tempo e del Disinganno (2007) and Lamenti (2008). In 2023 she conducted Handel's Giulio Cesare in Amsterdam, Purcell's The Indian Queen in Luxembourg and Mozart's Don Giovanni in Lille.

Haïm conducts Baroque music with great energy and a dramatic feeling for the theatre. She is one of the best-known female conductors of early music.
artiest/emmanuelle-haim.listen: Listen to Dido's Lament from Dido and Aeneas in the recording by Emmanuelle Haïm and notice the descending bass line that keeps returning. Can you hear how the voice slowly rises above it?

artiest/engelbert-humperdinck.text:
Engelbert Humperdinck's real name is Arnold Dorsey. He was born in Madras, in British India, in 1936, and at the age of ten moved with his family to Leicester. In the early 1950s he played saxophone in nightclubs, and only later began to sing. From 1959 he made records under the name Gerry Dorsey, but success eluded him. In 1961 he contracted tuberculosis and spent nine months in hospital.

In 1965 he teamed up with the manager Gordon Mills, who also looked after Tom Jones. Mills gave him the striking name of the German composer of the opera Hänsel und Gretel. His first success came in Belgium, where he won the Knokke song festival in 1966. In early 1967 his version of Release Me reached number 1 in England. The record kept The Beatles' Strawberry Fields Forever and Penny Lane off the top spot, the first time since 1963 that a Beatles single had failed to reach number 1. There Goes My Everything and The Last Waltz followed, and later, among others, A Man Without Love and Quando quando quando.

Humperdinck sings romantic ballads in a warm, full voice, accompanied by a large orchestra and choir. Release Me was arranged in an orchestral country style, with Jimmy Page among the session guitarists. He himself did not want to be called a crooner. Set against the innovative pop of 1967, his music stood for an older, more traditional audience, which remained loyal to him. In 2012 he sang for the United Kingdom at the Eurovision Song Contest.
artiest/engelbert-humperdinck.listen: Listen to Release Me and notice how the orchestra carries Humperdinck's voice. Hear how a full choir joins in on the third chorus, and compare the sound with Strawberry Fields Forever, the Beatles single he kept off the top spot.

artiest/english-baroque-soloists.text:
The English Baroque Soloists are a chamber orchestra that plays on period instruments. The ensemble was founded in 1978 and grew out of the Monteverdi Orchestra, which the conductor John Eliot Gardiner had formed in 1968 to accompany his Monteverdi Choir. That orchestra at first played on modern instruments. At the end of the 1970s it switched to instruments from the period itself and adopted the name English Baroque Soloists. The repertoire runs from the early Baroque to the Classical period.

The group soon began to record prolifically. Early recordings included Acis and Galatea (1978), Bach's motets (1981), Messiah and Water Music (1982), and Music for the Royal Fireworks (1984). The orchestra made the first recording of all of Mozart's piano concertos on period instruments, with Malcolm Bilson on the fortepiano, and recorded seven of Mozart's operas. It often performs with the Monteverdi Choir. In 1990 Gardiner also founded the Orchestre Révolutionnaire et Romantique, for later repertoire with partly the same players. In 2023 the orchestra played at the coronation of Charles III and Camilla in Westminster Abbey.

The English Baroque Soloists belong to the movement that plays early music with the instruments and playing styles of its own time, which produces a lighter, sharper and more agile sound than a modern symphony orchestra. In this way the orchestra helped to give Baroque music a place of its own in the record shop.
artiest/english-baroque-soloists.listen: Listen to Water Music in the recording by the English Baroque Soloists and notice the natural horns and the crisp, light strings. Can you hear how the rhythm of the dance is carried by the whole orchestra?

artiest/english-chamber-orchestra.text:
The English Chamber Orchestra, ECO for short, is a British chamber orchestra from London. As a full orchestra it regularly plays at Cadogan Hall, and as a smaller ensemble at Wigmore Hall. Its origins lie in the Goldsbrough Orchestra, which was founded in 1948 by Lawrence Leonard and Arnold Goldsbrough. In 1960 the name changed to English Chamber Orchestra, because the old name would have stood in the way of success outside England.

Shortly afterwards the orchestra became closely associated with the Aldeburgh Festival, where it took part in the first performances of Benjamin Britten's A Midsummer Night's Dream in 1960, Owen Wingrave in 1970 and Curlew River. For a long time it had no permanent principal conductor and worked with guest conductors such as Raymond Leppard, Colin Davis and Daniel Barenboim. In 1985 Jeffrey Tate became the first principal conductor. Ralf Gothóni and Paul Watkins, among others, followed later, and a new appointment was made in 2023. Its albums range from Dido and Aeneas (1961) and The Indian Queen (1966) to Britten's Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra (1967) and Handel's Wassermusik (1971). King Charles III has been its patron since 1977.

The ECO plays as a small, nimble orchestra on modern instruments, and has made many recordings of Baroque, Classical and twentieth-century English music. In this way the orchestra became a fixture of the British record industry from the 1960s to the 1980s.
artiest/english-chamber-orchestra.listen: Listen to Britten's Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra in the recording by the English Chamber Orchestra and notice how each instrument plays the theme on its own. Can you hear how the families of strings, woodwind and percussion make themselves heard one after another?

artiest/ennio-morricone.text: Ennio Morricone, from Rome, was a trumpeter and studied composition with Goffredo Petrassi. He first worked as an arranger of pop songs. With Sergio Leone's Per un pugno di dollari (1964) he found a new Western sound. Alongside the orchestra he used whistling, electric guitar, whip cracks, jew's harp, choir and screaming voices. In Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo (1966) each character has a sound of his own. Leone sometimes had scenes shot to music that was already finished. Morricone wrote well over four hundred scores, including for gialli and arthouse films. After an honorary Oscar in 2007, he won the Oscar for The Hateful Eight in 2016.
artiest/ennio-morricone.listen: Notice the unusual instruments alongside the orchestra: a whistled melody, electric guitar, whip, and voices used as an instrument.

artiest/enrico-caruso.text:
Enrico Caruso was born in Naples in 1873, into a poor but not destitute family. His father was a mechanic and foundry worker, and young Enrico too was first put to work in engineering. He sang in a church choir and in the street, took singing lessons and made his debut in 1895 at the Teatro Nuovo in Naples. After years in provincial opera houses he signed a contract with La Scala in 1900, where under Arturo Toscanini he sang the role of Rodolfo in La bohème.

The turning point came in 1902. In Milan he made his first series of records for the British Gramophone Company, ten in all, and they became bestsellers at once. In 1903 he made his debut at the Metropolitan Opera in New York, where he would remain the centre of attention for years. Puccini wrote the role of Dick Johnson in La fanciulla del West in 1910 with Caruso's voice in mind. During the First World War he sang extensively for charities and war-bond drives. He died in 1921 at the age of 48.

Caruso was a tenor with a very wide repertoire, from lyric to dramatic roles. Between 1902 and 1920 he made about 250 commercial recordings. That made him the first international recording star: a singer who reached his audience not only in the concert hall but also through the gramophone, even in living rooms where opera had never been heard. Later releases of his work, such as the collection Sacred Songs for the Holy Year from 1949, show how long his voice remained in circulation. Anyone who wants to understand the history of pop music as the history of recording will end up with him.
artiest/enrico-caruso.listen: Listen to one of his recordings from the years 1902 to 1920 and notice the power and warmth of the voice, despite the flat sound of early recording technology. Can you hear how he had to project his voice into the horn?

artiest/enrique-batiz.text:
Enrique Bátiz Campbell was a Mexican conductor and concert pianist, born in Mexico City in 1942. He began piano lessons at the age of eight and later studied in Dallas, at the Juilliard School in New York and in Warsaw, where he also learned conducting. From 1969 he concentrated on conducting. In 1971 he co-founded the Orquesta Sinfónica del Estado de México, which he led until 2018. In between, from 1983 to 1989, he was principal conductor of the Mexico City Philharmonic. In 1984 he became a guest conductor of the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra.

Bátiz made about 145 recordings, for labels such as EMI, ASV and Naxos, with orchestras in Mexico and Great Britain. He recorded the nine symphonies of Beethoven, the six of Tchaikovsky, symphonies by Schumann and Brahms, and the complete orchestral works of Joaquín Rodrigo. He also built up a series of eight volumes of Mexican music, with works by, among others, Manuel M. Ponce. He conducted the first digital recording of Villa-Lobos's Bachianas Brasileiras, for which Brazil awarded him the Rio Branco Medal in 1986.

His name appears above all in the budget CD repertoire of the 1980s and 1990s: the well-known symphonies, overtures and ballet suites in solid, accessible performances. That made classical music available to a large audience. His importance also lies in the Mexican repertoire, which he put on the map both at home and abroad. He died in 2025, after a career of more than fifty years.
artiest/enrique-batiz.listen: Listen to his recording of Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition and notice how an orchestra brings to life a series of short musical paintings, with the varied colours of the instrumental groups.

artiest/enrique-jorrin.text:
Enrique Jorrín was a Cuban violinist, composer and bandleader, born in 1926 in Candelaria, in the province of Pinar del Río. As a child he moved with his family to the Havana district of El Cerro, where he lived for the rest of his life. At the age of twelve he chose the violin and studied at the municipal conservatory of Havana. He played in the orchestra of the National Institute of Music, in 1941 in the danzonera of the Hermanos Contreras, and later in the charanga of Antonio Arcaño y sus Maravillas.

In the early 1950s he played in the Orquesta América of Ninón Mondéjar. There he devised a new dance style that became known as the cha-cha-chá and grew out of the danzón. Jorrín is therefore regarded as the inventor of the genre. From 1954 to 1958 he lived in Mexico, in 1964 he toured Africa and Europe with his own orchestra, and from that year he recorded extensively for the Cuban label EGREM. His compositions include the danzones Hilda and Silver Star and the cha-cha-chás La engañadora, El túnel and Nada para ti.

The charanga, with violin, flute and rhythm section, gave his music a light, danceable sound. Jorrín made the rhythm simpler than that of the danzón, so that even beginner dancers could join in. In this way he carried a Cuban form into ballrooms all over the world. In 1974 he founded a new charanga with the singer Tito Gómez and the pianist Rubén González. Jorrín died in Havana in 1987, but many of his songs are still in the repertoire of his orchestra.
artiest/enrique-jorrin.listen: Listen to a cha-cha-chá by Jorrín, for example La engañadora, and notice the calm, constantly recurring rhythm that you can easily count along with, and the role of the violin and flute in the charanga.

artiest/ensemble-al-kindi.text:
Ensemble Al-Kindî is a music group founded in Aleppo, Syria, in 1983 by Julien Jalâl Eddine Weiss. The name refers to Al-Kindi, a philosopher and music theorist from the Arab world. It began with three players: Weiss himself, the Egyptian tar and riqq player Adel Schams Eldin and the Syrian nay player Ziad Kadhi Amin. At first the group played only instrumental pieces. Later Weiss expanded the ensemble with singers, among them Sheikh Hamza Shakkûr, a well-known singer of classical music and leader of the Sufi community of the whirling dervishes. In 1986 Weiss converted to Islam and settled in Aleppo.

The ensemble wanted to build a repertoire from across the Arab world, and drew inspiration from Arab-Andalusian, Eastern, Turkish and Iranian traditions. Its records began to appear in 1989, among them Arab Classical Music, Sufi Songs of Damascus in 1993, Le Salon de Musique d'Alep in 1998 and The Whirling Dervishes of Damascus in 2000. Les croisades sus le regard de l'orient, Transe Soufie D'Alep and Parfums ottomans followed later.

The group plays oud, spike fiddle, flute, percussion and zither, often with devotional singing beneath. At concerts, real dervishes sometimes dance along. The ensemble introduced a classical and Sufi tradition to Europe that was little known there, and worked with soloists from Syria, Iraq, Turkey and Tunisia. Weiss died in 2015.
artiest/ensemble-al-kindi.listen: Listen to a recording by the ensemble, for example of the Sufi liturgy from Damascus, and notice how the singing is repeated again and again, and how the flute, string and percussion instruments follow that rhythm and tone.

artiest/ensemble-albalonga.text:
Ensemble Albalonga is an early-music ensemble about which very little has been recorded. It was led by the conductor Anibal Cetrangolo and in 2001 recorded, for the Belgian label Pavane, a three-CD set of Amor es todo invención: Júpiter y Anfitrión, a zarzuela from 1721 by Giacomo Facco to a libretto by José de Cañizares.

The discography shows where the group focused: Baroque music theatre and earlier opera. Besides Facco's zarzuela, Euridice (2000) and Peru - El Diamante were released. The three CDs were a substantial release for a work that was hardly known outside Spain. A zarzuela is a Spanish form of music theatre in which sung and spoken parts alternate.

Albalonga's work belongs to the movement that brings forgotten Baroque repertoire back to life in historically informed performances. Nothing has been recorded here about the ensemble's founding, its line-up or its precise instruments, and that information has yet to be researched.
artiest/ensemble-albalonga.listen: Listen to an excerpt from the recording of Euridice and notice how the singers are accompanied by a small Baroque ensemble instead of a large orchestra.

artiest/ensemble-birun-en-kudsi-erguner.text:
Kudsi Ergüner is a Turkish master of the ney, the reed flute that plays a major role in Sufi music, and Ensemble Bîrûn plays classical Ottoman music. To understand their work it helps to know the tradition. Ottoman music, also called Turkish classical music, is the classical music of the Ottoman Empire. It arose at the palace, in the great cities and in the Sufi lodges, and traditionally features a solo singer with a small to medium-sized instrumental ensemble.

The tradition reached its peak around the beginning of the eighteenth century and goes back to the music of the Hellenistic and Persian world. Its hallmark is the modal system of makams, in which melodic scales and the shape of the melody are laid down. In Ottoman music alone, more than six hundred makams have been used. Its forms include the peşrev, the kâr and the saz semaî. A peşrev is an instrumental opening piece, such as Acem Peşrev, which is written in a particular rhythmic cycle, here Usûl Devr-i Kebîr.

In the nineteenth century, Westernisation caused Western classical music to displace the native tradition. The Ottoman elite regarded their own music as primitive and underdeveloped next to Western music, and after the fall of the empire the new republican elite tried to push it back still further. Musicians such as Ergüner and ensembles such as Bîrûn keep the old tradition alive, with the characteristic sound of the ney, string instruments and percussion.
artiest/ensemble-birun-en-kudsi-erguner.listen: Listen to Acem Peşrev and notice how the melody moves in a flowing, winding line without chords. Can you hear how a fixed rhythmic pattern beneath it keeps the cycle?

artiest/ensemble-die-reihe.text:
Ensemble die reihe is a Viennese ensemble for new music. The group was founded in 1958 by the composers Friedrich Cerha and Kurt Schwertsik and played works of the twentieth-century avant-garde. The name has another meaning too: Die Reihe was a German journal on serial music, published between 1955 and 1962, and has no connection with this ensemble.

The recordings show a broad range of interests. A CD with Und Du... Verzeichnis Für K appeared in 2011, and a release with Couplets, Ballads, Orchestral Suites 2 to 4 and Die letzte Nacht in 2022. The name also turns up on recordings of Debussy, such as Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune, Nocturnes, Chansons de Bilitis and Jeux, and of music by Satie.

The ensemble belongs to the generation that cleared the way for new music in Vienna after the Second World War. It gave composers a permanent group of players who could perform their work, and provided a platform for music that had little chance in ordinary concert halls. Little is recorded in this source about its line-up and precise history, and that has yet to be researched.
artiest/ensemble-die-reihe.listen: Listen to the recording of Debussy or of Satie and notice how a small ensemble makes the music sound clear and transparent, without the full sound of a large orchestra.

artiest/ensemble-galilei.text:
Ensemble Galilei is an American group that combines early music, Celtic traditionals and new compositions. From 1987 it recorded a series of albums, beginning with The Mystic and the Muse. In the 1990s came Music in the Great Hall in 1992, and Ancient Noëls and Following the Moon in 1993. After that came Come, Gentle Night: Music of Shakespeare's World in 2000, From the Isles to the Courts in 2001 and A Winter's Night in 2002.

The group kept recording in later years too. From the Edge of the World appeared in 2007, A Change of Worlds in 2012, Surrounded by Angels: A Christmas Celebration with Ensemble Galilei in 2013 and From Whence We Came in 2015. The titles show where the ensemble focused: music from the British Isles and the Celtic world, the age of Shakespeare, and Christmas and winter repertoire.

The sound of such a group is chamber-musical. Strings, flutes and percussion create a soft, acoustic atmosphere in which medieval and Renaissance music sounds not like a museum piece but like living folk music. In this way the ensemble tapped into the interest in early and Celtic music that grew among a wide audience from the 1980s onwards. Nothing about its founding and line-up is recorded in the available source, and that has yet to be researched.
artiest/ensemble-galilei.listen: Listen to a track from the album A Winter's Night and notice the acoustic instruments and the calm, chamber-musical atmosphere in which the melody takes pride of place.

artiest/ensemble-intercontemporain.text:
The Ensemble intercontemporain, EIC for short, is a French ensemble in Paris devoted to contemporary music. Pierre Boulez founded it in 1976, with the support of the Minister of Culture Michel Guy and in collaboration with Nicholas Snowman. The idea came from Boulez's experiences in the post-war avant-garde at Darmstadt in the 1950s, where he worked with contemporaries such as Stockhausen, Berio, Ligeti and Nono. He missed places where new music could be played and promoted. The EIC consists of thirty-one permanent soloists and works closely with IRCAM, the Parisian institute for acoustic and musical research. Péter Eötvös was the first music director in 1979. Later directors included David Robertson and Jonathan Nott.

The ensemble plays some thirty times a year in Paris and tours in France and beyond. Its repertoire contains more than two thousand contemporary works, from Elliott Carter, Dallapiccola and Berio to the complete works of Boulez, Ligeti, Kurtág and George Benjamin. Much of it has been recorded. The recordings run from Kammermusik in 1978 to releases with Varèse, Ravel and Schoenberg's Verklärte Nacht.

The ensemble often commissions new pieces and works with composers on both creation and performance, because the new playing techniques and notation demand a great deal of coordination. It also gives workshops and masterclasses for young musicians. In this way it has grown into a model for ensembles that give contemporary music a permanent place in concert life.
artiest/ensemble-intercontemporain.listen: Listen to Varèse's Density 21.5 in the ensemble's recording and notice how a single flute carries the whole piece, from very soft to shrill and high.

artiest/ensemble-kerylos.text:
Ensemble Kérylos is a French ensemble that brings the music of classical antiquity to life. It was founded in the early 1990s by Annie Bélis, born in 1951, an archaeologist, philologist, papyrologist and musician, and a research director at the French CNRS. She specialises in the music of ancient Greece and Rome and herself studied piano, organ, flute and cello.

The aim was to recreate the music of antiquity as faithfully as possible, in three steps. First Bélis deciphered musical papyri, as part of her scholarly work. Then she had the ancient instruments rebuilt, on the basis of archaeological material and with the help of the French and Spanish instrument makers J.-C. Condi and C. Gonzalez. Finally the ensemble performed the scores. Bélis worked, among other things, on a papyrus containing a Paean to Apollo by Mesomedes of Crete, and on a papyrus with a version of Medea by Carcinus, in which Medea does not kill her children.

The recordings Musiques de l'antiquité grecque (1996) and D'Euripide Aux Premiers Chrétiens (2016) let us hear the result. The sound is that of lyre, kithara and wind instruments, with singing in a strange-sounding scale. In this way the ensemble gives an impression of a musical world that we know only from fragments. The reconstructions remain scholarly hypotheses, but they make the oldest Western notation audible.
artiest/ensemble-kerylos.listen: Listen to an excerpt from Musiques de l'antiquité grecque and notice the sound of the ancient string and wind instruments and how different the melody sounds from modern music.

artiest/ensemble-kerylos-annie-belis.text:
Ensemble Kérylos plays music from classical antiquity, as close as possible to how it sounded then. The group was founded in the early 1990s by the French researcher Annie Bélis, born in 1951. She is an archaeologist, philologist and papyrologist, and works as a research director at the French CNRS. She studied in Paris and Athens and took her doctorate at the Sorbonne. She is also a musician herself: she learned to play piano, organ, flute and cello.

The ensemble's work begins with the sources. Bélis deciphers music preserved on ancient papyri and stones, in a Greek musical notation. She then had the instruments of the time rebuilt with French and Spanish instrument makers, such as the lyre and the kithara, on the basis of archaeological finds. Only then can the ensemble play the pieces. In 1996 the CD De la pierre au son: Musiques de l'Antiquité grecque et romaine appeared. In 2016 came D'Euripide aux premiers chrétiens, with new performances based on more recent research and the first recording of a reconstructed Roman kithara.

Kérylos's recordings let us hear how far back the history of sung melodies goes. The fragment from Euripides' Orestes dates from the fifth century BC, the first Delphic Hymn from the second century BC, and the Epitaph of Seikilos from around the year 100. It remains a reconstruction: nobody knows exactly how this music sounded, but Bélis tries, with scientific evidence, to come as close as possible.
artiest/ensemble-kerylos-annie-belis.listen: Listen to Épitaphe de Seikilos, a short song that was preserved on a gravestone. Notice how the melody moves in calm steps and how short and rounded the song is.

artiest/ensemble-musica-nova.text:
Musica Nova is a French early-music ensemble founded in 2000. It brings together singers and instrumentalists under the direction of the singer and conductor Lucien Kandel. The repertoire runs from the Middle Ages to the Baroque and is driven by the wish to convey emotion through music.

The ensemble works with an eye for historical accuracy. It uses original manuscripts and pays attention to the rules of the time, such as musica ficta and pronunciation, and to the nuances the composer intended. The singers and musicians read their parts in facsimile, which inevitably changes their interpretation. Musica Nova performs in France and beyond.

The recordings let us hear that repertoire. Les Motets appeared in 2002, Flos florum in 2005, Missa cuiusvis toni in 2007, Ballades in 2009 and Se congie prens in 2013. The titles point to the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the age of the French ballades and the motets. According to the source, some recordings have become a benchmark for how this style is now performed. In this way the ensemble contributes to the rediscovery of a music that remained almost invisible for centuries.
artiest/ensemble-musica-nova.listen: Listen to an excerpt from Ballades and notice how a few voices and instruments each follow a melodic line of their own, without the broad orchestral sound we know from later music.

artiest/ensemble-organum.text:
Ensemble Organum is a French early-music ensemble founded in 1982 by Marcel Pérès. Its make-up has varied over the years. Its singers have included Josep Cabré, Josep Benet, Gérard Lesne, Antoine Sicot and Malcolm Bothwell. The group often worked with the Greek singer Lycourgos Angelopoulos. The ensemble was first based at the abbey of Sénanque and later at Royaumont. Since 2001 it has shared a site on the grounds of the abbey of Moissac with a centre for research into early music.

Organum focuses mainly on music from the Middle Ages: Beneventan, Old Roman, Gallican, Carolingian and Mozarabic chant. Renaissance polyphony and more recent works are also heard. The influence of Orthodox chant is audible. The group also works with musicologists and historians on research into this repertoire.

The discography begins in 1984 with Polyphonie aquitaine du XIIe siècle: Saint Martial de Limoges. Among the releases that followed were École Notre-Dame: Messe du Jour de Noël, Chants de l'église milanaise, Carmina Burana in 1990, Codex Faenza from fifteenth-century Italy and Chant Cistercien in 1992. The ensemble showed how broad medieval church music was and that it sounds less familiar than the well-known Gregorian chants.
artiest/ensemble-organum.listen: Listen to a recording by Organum of medieval chant and notice the long, sustained notes and how different voices slowly build up a sound together.

artiest/ensemble-rustavi.text:
The Rustavi Ensemble, also called the Georgian State Academic Ensemble, is a Georgian folk music ensemble founded in 1968 by Anzor Erkomaishvili. He was a singer and folklorist from a Georgian musical family going back seven generations. Since its founding, Rustavi has performed in more than fifty countries. The ensemble sings and dances: songs and dances for work and war, in splendid costumes and with elaborate choreography.

Its hallmark is Georgian polyphonic singing, in which voices slide over one another and harmonies are constantly in motion. The ensemble's sacred hymns also have those overlapping sounds. Erkomaishvili wanted to break through the boundaries between the regional styles and yet present ethnographically authentic music from all over Georgia. In this way Rustavi combines the powerful, rough sound of the traditional regional choirs with a newer, cleaner aesthetic aimed at the concert stage. The singers try to preserve, and sometimes recreate, the original vocal colours, but they simplified the complicated scales of the older choirs to obtain firmer, clearer harmonies. Sometimes a smaller group sings, so that the structure of a song is easier to hear.

In 2001 the ensemble received the UNESCO Pacha Prize for the preservation and dissemination of Georgian polyphonic singing in Georgia. Rustavi has also made that vocal heritage known outside Georgia.
artiest/ensemble-rustavi.listen: Listen to Mravalzhamieri and notice how the voices move over one another rather than as a single melody with accompaniment. Can you follow the different voices separately, and where do they come together?

artiest/ensemble-shashmaqam.text:
Shashmaqam is a musical genre from Central Asia, characteristic of Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, which probably originated in the city of Bukhara. In Persian the word means the six maqams, the modes on which the music is based. It is a refined music with texts taken from Sufi poets on divine love. The instruments accompany the voices sparingly. Usually there are a few long-necked lutes, such as the rawap, tar, tanbur or dutar, the dayra, a frame drum with jingling discs that resembles a tambourine, and the sato, a bowed tanbur.

In the first half of the twentieth century, Abdul Rauf Fitrat wrote a book in 1927 in which he presented the shashmaqam as the great musical tradition of the Uzbek people. In the 1930s, under Stalin, the music was regarded with suspicion, and from the mid-1950s it was ideologically rehabilitated. Tajikistan and Uzbekistan each regarded the music as their own heritage, and in Dushanbe and Tashkent a tradition of its own developed. In the 1980s that artificial separation began to change.

The Bukharan Jews brought the shashmaqam to the West, especially to the United States. Many of them were successful performers. An ensemble like this one lets us hear how old and sophisticated the classical music of Central Asia is, with a system of modes of its own that stands beside the Persian and Turkish traditions.
artiest/ensemble-shashmaqam.listen: Listen to Talqin-i Bayat and notice the singing and the sparse accompaniment of lute and frame drum. How does the melody follow a fixed mode, and how does the drum keep the rhythm?

artiest/epica.text:
Epica is a Dutch symphonic metal band. Guitarist and singer Mark Jansen started the group in 2002, after leaving After Forever at the age of 23. He was looking for musicians for a classical and symphonic project, at first called Sahara Dust. Simone Simons became the singer, and the name Epica came from an album by the band Kamelot. With a choir and a small string orchestra the group made a two-song demo in 2002, Cry for the Moon, which led to a record contract.

The debut album The Phantom Agony appeared in 2003 and produced the single Cry for the Moon. Among the albums that followed were Consign to Oblivion (2005), for which film composers such as Hans Zimmer and Danny Elfman were an inspiration, The Divine Conspiracy (2007), Design Your Universe (2009) and The Quantum Enigma (2014). Epica's sound revolves around contrasts: Simons's classical-sounding soprano against Jansen's grunts, and heavy metal guitars against orchestral parts and operatic choirs. Later, influences from death metal, progressive metal and Arabic music were added. The lyrics often deal with philosophy, religion, science and politics.

Epica became one of the Dutch bands with the most success abroad. In 2015 the group received the Music Export Award, the prize for the Dutch act that had performed best internationally the year before. Together with Within Temptation, Epica shows that the Netherlands has a strong place in symphonic metal.
artiest/epica.listen: Listen to Cry for the Moon and notice how the clear, classical-sounding vocals of Simone Simons, the choir and the strings relate to the heavy guitars and drums.

artiest/erasure.text:
Erasure is an English synth-pop duo that began in London in 1985. Vince Clarke already had a remarkable career behind him. He co-founded Depeche Mode and wrote their breakthrough hit Just Can't Get Enough, and then formed the duo Yazoo with Alison Moyet. For a new project he placed an advertisement in the magazine Melody Maker. The singer Andy Bell from Peterborough responded and was chosen. Clarke was his hero.

The first three singles and the debut album Wonderland (1986) did little in England. That changed with the fourth single, Sometimes, which reached number 2 at the end of 1986. A long run of hits followed, such as Victim of Love, Ship of Fools, A Little Respect, Stop!, Blue Savannah, Chorus and Always. The Innocents (1988) was the first of five English number 1 albums in a row. With the EP Abba-esque (1992), four ABBA covers, they had their first number 1 single, and the video with the duo in ABBA outfits helped set off the ABBA revival of the 1990s. In 1989 Erasure received the Brit Award for best British group.

Erasure's music is cheerful, melodic electronic pop. Clarke makes the sounds with synthesizers, Bell sings the melody. They name OMD, Kraftwerk, Gloria Gaynor and ABBA as influences. Between 1986 and 2007, 24 singles in a row reached the English top 40. After 2000 too, the duo kept making records together.
artiest/erasure.listen: Listen to Sometimes and notice the acoustic guitar that comes through between the synthesizers. Hear how the song nevertheless remains clearly synth-pop, with Andy Bell's vocals up front.

artiest/eric-b-en-rakim.text:
Eric B. & Rakim was a hip hop duo from New York, with DJ Eric B. and rapper Rakim. Eric Barrier came from Queens. At school he played trumpet and drums, switched to turntables and became a DJ at the radio station WBLS. Looking for a rapper, he was led by a promoter to William Griffin from Wyandanch on Long Island, who called himself Rakim. In a basement Eric B. began mixing records for him. Their first single, Eric B. Is President (1986), he built on the bass line of Over Like a Fat Rat by Fonda Rae.

The debut album Paid in Full appeared in 1987, recorded in about a week. Rakim often wrote his lyrics on the spot in the studio. Singles such as I Ain't No Joke and I Know You Got Soul used samples of James Brown, and a remix of Paid in Full by the British duo Coldcut made them known in Europe too. Follow the Leader (1988), with Lyrics of Fury and Microphone Fiend, Let the Rhythm Hit 'Em (1990) and Don't Sweat the Technique (1992) followed. After a business dispute they split up.

Where rappers such as Run-DMC and Chuck D shouted loudly and energetically, Rakim rapped slowly and with control, letting every line fall emphatically. Eric B. looked for loops and samples full of soul, and in doing so pointed the way for many later producers. For many they were the best DJ-and-rapper duo of hip hop's golden years. Their own work was in turn sampled, among others in Pump Up the Volume by M|A|R|R|S.
artiest/eric-b-en-rakim.listen: Listen to Paid in Full and notice the difference between the two: Eric B. builds a tight beat out of samples, while Rakim raps calmly and precisely over it. Hear how Rakim hardly raises his voice, and yet draws all the attention.

artiest/eric-burdon.text:
Eric Burdon was born in 1941 in Walker, a working-class district of Newcastle upon Tyne. His school years were hard, but a teacher helped him get to art college, where he studied graphic design and photography. There he met the drummer John Steel. With his friends he hung around the jazz club The Downbeat and listened to American music. In 1962 he joined the band of the organist Alan Price as singer, and shortly afterwards it became known as The Animals.

The Animals mixed electric blues with rock and became one of the most important bands of the British Invasion in America, alongside The Beatles and The Rolling Stones. Burdon's powerful voice can be heard on The House of the Rising Sun, Don't Let Me Be Misunderstood, We Gotta Get Out of This Place, It's My Life and Don't Bring Me Down. After Price and the others left, he continued in California as Eric Burdon and the Animals, with psychedelic hits such as San Franciscan Nights, Monterey and Sky Pilot, a song against the war in Vietnam.

In 1969 Burdon joined a funk band in San Francisco that came to be called Eric Burdon and War, with the hit Spill the Wine. Burdon is regarded as one of the most striking singers of the British Invasion, with a deep, raw blues voice and fierce performances. He was friends with Jimi Hendrix and John Lennon. In 2008 Rolling Stone placed him at number 57 on its list of the greatest singers of all time.
artiest/eric-burdon.listen: Listen to The House of the Rising Sun by The Animals and follow Eric Burdon's vocals. Hear how he begins quietly and sings with growing fierceness, until the song reaches its climax towards the end.

artiest/eric-clapton.text:
Eric Clapton was born in 1945 in Ripley, in the English county of Surrey. He belongs to the generation of British guitarists who discovered American blues in the 1960s and brought it to a rock audience with loud amplifiers. In 1967 an unknown fan in London wrote 'Clapton is God' on a wall. Clapton is the only person to have been inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame three times: as a solo artist, with The Yardbirds and with Cream.

From 1963 to 1965 he played in The Yardbirds. Then he joined John Mayall & the Bluesbreakers. The album Blues Breakers with Eric Clapton (1966) is known to fans as the 'Beano album', because on the cover Clapton is reading a comic. On it he played a 1960 Gibson Les Paul through an overdriven Marshall amplifier. That combination produced a thick, long-sustaining guitar tone that many guitarists after him sought. Still in 1966 he started the trio Cream with the bassist Jack Bruce and the drummer Ginger Baker, which broke up in November 1968. Blind Faith (1969) followed, and Derek and the Dominos, with the album Layla and Other Assorted Love Songs (1970).

The loud blues rock of Cream became a foundation for the hard rock of the 1970s. Clapton also played as a guest with others, such as the guitar solo in While My Guitar Gently Weeps by The Beatles. He wrote Tears in Heaven after the death of his little son Conor in 1991. It appears on Unplugged, an acoustic concert from 1992 that reached number 1 on the album chart in America.
artiest/eric-clapton.listen: Hideaway (1966) is an instrumental by Freddie King and Sonny Thompson. Notice how Clapton's notes hang in the air and distort slightly: that is the Les Paul through a Marshall turned up full, the sound that would define blues rock.

artiest/eric-dolphy.text: Eric Dolphy, from Los Angeles, played alto saxophone, flute and bass clarinet, an instrument that he was one of the first to use as a solo instrument in jazz. Charlie Parker was his starting point, but his lines made great leaps and sounded like birdsong. He played with Charles Mingus, John Coltrane and Ornette Coleman, and in 1964 recorded Out to Lunch! for Blue Note, with vibraphone and free forms. In June 1964 he recorded a session in Hilversum for the VARA with the pianist Misha Mengelberg and the drummer Han Bennink, released as Last Date. A few weeks later he died in Berlin of undiagnosed diabetes.
artiest/eric-dolphy.listen: Hear the great leaps in the melody, from very low to very high.

artiest/erich-wolfgang-korngold.text: Erich Wolfgang Korngold was born in Brno in 1897 and grew up in Vienna. As a child he was already considered a prodigy, and his opera Die tote Stadt (1920) became an international success. In 1934 the director Max Reinhardt brought him to Hollywood. After the Anschluss in 1938 he stayed there. For Warner Bros. Korngold wrote scores like operas without singing, with the rich harmonies of Strauss and Puccini. Captain Blood (1935) and The Sea Hawk (1940) are swashbuckling pirate adventures. Anthony Adverse (1936) and The Adventures of Robin Hood (1938) were awarded an Oscar. The main theme of Kings Row (1942) is often cited as an example for the style of John Williams.
artiest/erich-wolfgang-korngold.listen: Listen to the swashbuckling brass fanfares and the broad string melody: the orchestra sings as in an opera, while the action simply carries on.

artiest/erik-satie.text: Erik Satie earned his living as a pianist in the cabarets of Montmartre and later lived in a sparse little room in Arcueil. Against the heavy music of Wagner he set short, bare pieces with strange titles and mocking performance directions. His three Gymnopédies of 1888 repeat a calm accompaniment above which a simple melody floats. Debussy orchestrated two of them, and later Cage and the minimalists saw him as a forerunner.
artiest/erik-satie.listen: Listen to the first Gymnopédie and hear how the left hand keeps repeating the same two rocking chords, while the melody floats slowly over them.

artiest/erika-haase.text:
Erika Haase was a German classical pianist, born in Darmstadt in 1935, the daughter of a violinist. She received her first piano lessons at the age of seven and studied in Darmstadt with Werner Hoppstock and Hans Leygraf. In 1959 she won the Kranichsteiner Musikpreis of the city of Darmstadt in the piano category. She performed as a soloist and chamber musician with Swedish radio and with Swedish orchestras, and in 1960 attended the summer courses of Eduard Steuermann.

Her emphasis lay on Neue Musik. From 1963 to 1967 she lived for long periods between London and Paris, where she worked with the BBC and with Pierre Boulez. She maintained a close friendship with György Ligeti. From 1967 until her retirement in 2000 she taught at the Hanover University of Music, from 1974 as a permanent piano teacher. Her students included Gerrit Zitterbart, Andreas Staier and Ingo Metzmacher.

On record she is best known for a series of Études pour piano in five volumes, released between 1997 and 2012. She also recorded an album of works for piano and harpsichord. Haase belongs to the pianists who played the music of their own time as living repertoire and who passed on that knowledge to a next generation, among them a conductor such as Metzmacher. She died in Frankfurt in 2013.
artiest/erika-haase.listen: Listen to one of her Études pour piano and notice how each piece works out one particular pianistic problem, such as fast figures, chords or a special touch.

artiest/erma-franklin.text:
Erma Franklin was born in 1938 in Shelby, Mississippi, the eldest daughter of the Reverend C. L. Franklin. She grew up in Detroit, where her father was pastor of the New Bethel Baptist Church. There she sang as a child with her sisters Aretha and Carolyn. When Aretha began making records, Erma went on tour with her as a backing singer. She sings along on Respect, her sister's best-known song. She also studied business administration at Clark College in Atlanta.

In 1967 Erma Franklin was the first to record Piece of My Heart, written by Jerry Ragovoy and Bert Berns, who also produced it. It became a soul hit in the United States and earned her a Grammy nomination. A year later Janis Joplin recorded the song with Big Brother and the Holding Company. Erma later said that at first she did not recognise Joplin's version on the radio. In 1992 her own version became a hit again in England, after it was used in a jeans advertisement.

As a solo singer she never had the success of Aretha, partly because her record company found few suitable songs for her. In the mid-1970s she gave up music. She then worked for 25 years for an organisation in Detroit that helped homeless and disadvantaged children. Erma Franklin died in 2002.
artiest/erma-franklin.listen: Listen to Piece of My Heart by Erma Franklin and then to the version by Janis Joplin. Notice how Erma sings the song as a soul number, and how different the vocal outbursts sound in Joplin's rock version.

artiest/ernest-ansermet.text:
Ernest Ansermet was a Swiss conductor, born in Vevey in 1883. He began as a professor of mathematics at the University of Lausanne and in 1912 started conducting at the casino in Montreux. From 1915 to 1923 he led Diaghilev's Ballets Russes. Travelling for the company, he met Debussy and Ravel, with whom he discussed the performance of their works. During the First World War he got to know Igor Stravinsky, who was living in exile in Switzerland. There his lifelong bond with Russian music began.

In 1918 he founded the Orchestre de la Suisse Romande. He became known for precise performances of difficult modern music. After the Second World War he and his orchestra obtained a long-term contract with Decca, and until his death he recorded the greater part of his repertoire, often two or three times. His records include Petrushka in 1950, Le Sacre du printemps in 1951 and the complete ballet Daphnis et Chloé in 1953, as well as Debussy's La Mer and Beethoven's Ninth Symphony. His readings were clear and authoritative, although the orchestra did not always reach the highest international level.

Ansermet was one of the first in the classical world to take jazz seriously: in 1919 he wrote an article in which he praised Sidney Bechet. He played Stravinsky's works in their original version and disapproved of the composer's revisions. He avoided the music of Schoenberg and his circle entirely, and wrote a book against it, which damaged his reputation after the war. His importance lies in his recordings of Stravinsky, Debussy and Ravel, with which he spread ballet and modern music early on.
artiest/ernest-ansermet.listen: Listen to his 1951 recording of Le Sacre du printemps and notice how sharply and clearly the rhythmic blocks and the dissonant chords are worked out.

artiest/ernest-irving.text:
Kelville Ernest Irving was an English musical director, conductor and composer, born in Godalming, Surrey, in 1878. As a child he sang in the church choir, attended Charterhouse and taught himself the rest. His career began with applying for vacancies in The Stage. In 1895 he conducted his first orchestra, for a musical burlesque in Maidenhead. For twenty years he toured the country, by his own account with third-rate opera and second-rate musical comedy. In 1907 he made an arrangement of Tom Jones for fifteen players for Edward German, and the following year of Merrie England.

His breakthrough came in 1917, when he met Norman O'Neill at the Savage Club. O'Neill was musical director of the Haymarket Theatre and Irving stood in for him. From the end of the First World War until the end of the 1940s he was a fixture of London theatre. He conducted and composed for operettas, musicals and plays. An early success was the British version of Lilac Time in 1922, which ran for 626 performances. In 1928 he directed the music for Noël Coward's This Year of Grace, which ran for ten months.

His best-known work was done afterwards, for film. From the 1930s to the 1950s he was musical director of Ealing Studios. In this way he shaped the sound of British film of that time. He died in 1953.
artiest/ernest-irving.listen: Listen to the music for a British film from Ealing Studios of the 1940s or 1950s and notice how the music colours a scene and fixes the tone of the film.

artiest/ernest-ranglin.text:
Ernest Ranglin is a Jamaican guitarist and composer, born in Manchester, Jamaica, in 1932. His family moved to Kingston. He came to know the guitar through two uncles, and was largely self-taught. At fifteen he was already playing in the orchestra of Val Bennett, then in that of Eric Deans. That is how he met the jazz pianist Monty Alexander, with whom he formed a lifelong friendship and many collaborations.

In the 1950s he played on calypso and mento recordings, partly for the tourist market. From 1958 to 1965 he was a guitarist with the Jamaica Broadcasting Corporation. He recorded for Coxsone Dodd, including the hit Easy Snapping by Theophilus Beckford, which he arranged. As a studio guitarist and musical director he worked for labels such as Studio One and Island Records and played on many early ska recordings. He helped shape the rhythm guitar style that characterises ska. He worked with Jimmy Cliff, Prince Buster, the Skatalites and Bob Marley. Under his own name he released, among others, A Mod A Mod Ranglin in 1966, Boss Reggae in 1969, Below the Bassline in 1996 and Modern Answers to Old Problems in 2000.

His style combines jazz, mento and reggae, with chordal playing and rhythmic, percussive solos with influences from rhythm and blues and jazz. In this way he built a bridge between Jamaican folk music and jazz. In 2021 he received the Order of Jamaica.
artiest/ernest-ranglin.listen: Listen to a ska or reggae track on which Ranglin plays and notice the short, sharp guitar chords on the offbeat, which form the heart of the ska sound.

artiest/ernst-busch.text:
Ernst Busch was a German singer and actor, born in Kiel in 1900 into a working-class family. He first worked in a shipyard before using his talent for the stage and for singing. In the Berlin cabaret of the 1920s he broke through as an interpreter of political songs, above all those of Kurt Tucholsky. In 1928 he appeared in the original production of Bertolt Brecht's Dreigroschenoper and in 1931 in Pabst's film version. In the film Kuhle Wampe he sang the Solidaritätslied.

Busch was a communist all his life. In 1933 he fled Nazi Germany, first to the Netherlands, then to the Soviet Union. In 1937 he joined the International Brigades in Spain, and his war songs were broadcast by Radio Barcelona and Radio Madrid. After the fall of the Republic he was interned in Belgium and later imprisoned in France and Berlin. In 1945 the Red Army freed him. He settled in East Berlin, founded his own record label and worked with Brecht and Erwin Piscator at the Berliner Ensemble.

In the GDR he became a beloved figure, known as Galileo in Brecht's Leben des Galilei and as a singer of workers' songs, including many songs by Hanns Eisler. He also sang a remarkable version of Peat Bog Soldiers. His voice is raw and direct, meant to convey a message. His releases include Chronik in Liedern, Kantaten und Balladen in several volumes and Ernst Busch singt Brecht. He shows how closely politics and song could be intertwined in the twentieth century. He died in 1980.
artiest/ernst-busch.listen: Listen to Peat Bog Soldiers in Busch's performance and notice how he almost speaks the text, with a march rhythm that drives the song forward.

artiest/ernst-jansz.text:
Ernst Jansz was born in Amsterdam on 24 May 1948 and grew up in the Rivierenbuurt. His father was an Indo from Semarang on Java, who was in the Resistance during the war and ended up in a German concentration camp. Bob Dylan, The Beatles and Frédéric Chopin were his great musical examples. Before Doe Maar he played in the folk band CCC Inc.

Jansz was one of the founders of Doe Maar, the Dutch ska and reggae band that grew into one of the most successful groups in Dutch pop history. He was first asked as a keyboard player and played synthesizer on many tracks. Together with Henny Vrienten he wrote most of the songs, and the two took turns as lead singer. For the album Skunk he wrote Rumah Saya, about the feeling of not entirely belonging anywhere, neither in the Netherlands nor in Indonesia. In 1982 Doe Maar became enormously popular, but two years later the band split up under the pressure of all the fuss. In 2000 a last album followed, with occasional reunion concerts after that.

After Doe Maar, Jansz returned to CCC Inc. and from 1995 played in the backing band of Boudewijn de Groot. He made solo albums such as De Overkant (1999) and Molenbeekstraat (2006) and wrote novels, partly autobiographical. In them his Indisch background and the history of his father are central. He also published a book with translations of lyrics by Bob Dylan.
artiest/ernst-jansz.listen: Listen to Rumah Saya by Doe Maar. Notice the lyrics: Jansz sings about the country of his birth with no mountains on the horizon, and about the country of his father, where he would also be a stranger. Notice too the Indonesian words with which he asks where his home actually is.

artiest/ernst-reijseger.text:
Ernst Reijseger is a Dutch cellist and composer, born in Bussum in 1954. He began playing the cello at the age of eight and was taught by Anner Bijlsma at the Fontijnschool in Bussum. He plays avant-garde jazz, free jazz, improvised music and contemporary classical music, and often gives solo concerts. He has worked with, among others, Han Bennink, Misha Mengelberg, Derek Bailey, Louis Sclavis, Yo-Yo Ma, Albert Mangelsdorff and Joëlle Léandre.

He was for years a member of the ICP Orchestra of the Instant Composers Pool and plays in the Clusone Trio with Michael Moore and Han Bennink. He is also part of the Amsterdam String Trio and of the trio Graewe, Reijseger, Hemingway. His best-known solo album is Colla Parte from 1997, recorded in a villa in Sardinia. On that same trip he met the Voches de Sardinia, with whom he made Colla Voche. With Mola Sylla from Senegal he recorded Requiem for a Dying Planet and Janna. He also worked with musicians from Turkey, Iran and Argentina and with the Dutch group Boi Akih.

Reijseger also wrote film music, above all for Werner Herzog, including for The White Diamond, Cave of Forgotten Dreams and Salt and Fire. Herzog called him a great cellist who can do anything with his instrument. In this way Reijseger builds bridges between improvisation, film music and world music.
artiest/ernst-reijseger.listen: Listen to Colla Parte and notice how a single cello provides melody, rhythm and tone colour alike, from soft, bowed lines to pinched and plucked sounds.

artiest/erykah-badu.text:
Erykah Badu's real name is Erica Abi Wright, and she was born in Dallas, Texas, in 1971. At the age of four she was already on stage with her mother, an actress, and as a teenager she rapped live on a local radio station. She changed her first name to Erykah because she saw Erica as a slave name. She chose Badu because it was her favourite scat sound from jazz. After studying theatre she turned to music. In 1994 she opened for D'Angelo, and the manager Kedar Massenburg gave her a record contract.

In 1997 her debut Baduizm appeared, with On & On, Appletree and Next Lifetime. The album made her one of the figureheads of neo-soul and earned her the nickname Queen of Neo Soul. Her voice was often compared with that of Billie Holiday: low, languid and playful with the rhythm. That same year the live album Live appeared, with Tyrone. Mama's Gun (2000), with Bag Lady, Worldwide Underground (2003) and the two parts of New Amerykah (2008 and 2010) followed.

Badu combines soul and R&B with hip hop and jazz. She belonged to the Soulquarians, a circle of musicians around D'Angelo and Questlove who made records together. With her large, colourful headwraps she also had a recognisable look. Besides her music she played roles in films such as The Cider House Rules and Blues Brothers 2000.
artiest/erykah-badu.listen: Listen to On and On and notice the relaxed, slow groove and the way Badu sings just behind the beat. Can you hear why critics compare her voice with that of the jazz singer Billie Holiday?
